concept.name: Logistic regression
concept.definition: A regression model for a binary outcome that models the log-odds of the event as a linear function of the predictors, so predicted probabilities stay bounded between 0 and 1. Developed in its modern form by Cox (1958) and estimated by maximum likelihood rather than least squares.
concept.intuition: Instead of predicting the 0/1 outcome directly, predict the odds of the event on a log scale, where a straight line makes sense, then squash the result back to a probability with the logistic curve.
concept.mechanics: logit P(y=1|x) = beta_0 + x'beta, fitted by maximizing the Bernoulli log-likelihood; exponentiated coefficients give odds ratios per unit change in a predictor. Inference uses Wald, likelihood-ratio, or score tests, and fit is assessed with deviance and pseudo-R-squared measures.
concept.formula: P(y=1|x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(beta_0 + beta_1 x_1 + ... + beta_k x_k))); the log-odds log(p/(1-p)) = beta_0 + x'beta.
concept.failure_modes: Complete or quasi-complete separation (a predictor perfectly splits the outcomes) makes the MLEs diverge, and rare events bias small-sample estimates. The linear-in-log-odds form misses interactions and nonlinearities unless they are added explicitly.
concept.misconceptions: That the coefficients are marginal effects on probability: they are effects on log-odds, and the probability effect varies with x, equal to beta_j p(1-p).
concept.example: Modeling whether a stock beats the index next month (1/0) from momentum and valuation z-scores: exp(beta) for momentum is the multiplicative change in the odds of outperformance per z-score unit.
